text.text: Acquiescence (ACQ), the tendency to agree regardless of item content, can differ across groups and thereby mimic or mask measurement non-invariance.
Model-based recursive partitioning (MOB) combined with factor-analytic models (e.g.
EFAtree, CFAtree) is increasingly used to detect non-invariance across many covariates, but whether the detected heterogeneity can be attributed to its correct source is unknown.

In a Monte Carlo simulation (432 conditions, 500 replications each), we compared EFAtree and CFAtree with their randomintercept (RI) versions under four data-generating conditions: groups differed in neither source, in ACQ only, in the content loadings only, or in both.
We also propose a block-wise efficient score test that separates instability in the RI variance from instability in the content loadings by projecting out all other parameters.
All trees held the nominal Type I error rate.

When groups differed only in ACQ, trees without an RI factor mistook the difference for metric non-invariance under unbalanced keying or missed it under balanced keying, whereas the RI trees detected it regardless of keying.

Applied to the true grouping variable, the standard block test, which selects a block from the fully decorrelated scores, attributed purely substantive non-invariance to ACQ in 79% of replications, more often in larger samples.
The efficient test kept this misattribution near the nominal level (.06) and attributed heterogeneity correctly at the attainable maximum.
With one content factor, EFA-and CFA-based trees produced identical results.

In an empirical example with the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (N = 26236), the RI variance differed across countries but not across age groups or genders, and even across countries it was only one of several unstable parameter blocks, alongside the intercepts and the factor-mean and factorvariance directions.
Before a split is interpreted as measurement non-invariance, its source should be examined with an RI factor and efficient block-wise tests.
Acquiescence (ACQ) is the tendency of respondents to agree with items on a scale without paying attention to their content (Jackson & Messick, 1958 , 1961).

text.text: Several approaches are available for testing MI.
In the following section, we describe two factor-analytic approaches-confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and exploratory factor analysis (EFA)-along with their tree-based extensions in detail.
Confirmatory factor analysis with multiple groups (MGCFA) is one of the most commonly used methods for testing MI.
In this approach, MI is evaluated across four nested steps: configural, metric, scalar, and strict (residual).
These steps are conducted sequentially, with each model compared to the preceding one.
If model-data fit deteriorates as additional equality constraints are imposed, MI is considered to be violated (Schoot et al., 2012).
text.formatted: If model-data fit deteriorates as additional equality constraints are imposed, MI is considered to be violated <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Schoot et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The comparison of nested models is typically based on changes in various fit indices (Kline, 2023).
text.formatted: The comparison of nested models is typically based on changes in various fit indices <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Kline, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: There is ongoing debate regarding which fit indices should be reported and which cut-off criteria best indicate non-invariance.
One widely used recommendation is a threshold of ΔCFI ≤ -0.01 for the Comparative Fit Index (Cheung & Rensvold, 2002).
text.formatted: One widely used recommendation is a threshold of ΔCFI ≤ -0.01 for the Comparative Fit Index <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cheung & Rensvold, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, several criteria have been proposed for the Standardized Root Mean Square Residual (ΔSRMR) and the Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (ΔRMSEA).
For further details, see Chen (2007), Rutkowski and Svetina (2014), and Putnick and Bornstein (2016).
text.formatted: For further details, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Chen (2007)</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Rutkowski and Svetina (2014)</ref>, and <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Putnick and Bornstein (2016)</ref>.

text.text: Despite its widespread use, MGCFA has several limitations for testing MI.

First, when multiple covariates are present in a dataset, MI must be tested separately for each one, which can be time-consuming; moreover, analyzing each covariate independently ignores potential interaction effects (e.g., gender × region).
Second, as the number of groups increases, multiple-CFA to Test MI comparison problems may lead to incorrect identification of the source of non-invariance (Rutkowski & Svetina, 2014).
text.formatted: Second, as the number of groups increases, multiple-CFA to Test MI comparison problems may lead to incorrect identification of the source of non-invariance <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Rutkowski & Svetina, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Third, MGCFA is not well suited to handling continuous covariates.
These limitations have motivated the development of alternative approaches.
For example, Asparouhov and Muthén (2014) introduced the alignment optimization method, which accommodates a large number of groups but allows only a single categorical covariate.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Asparouhov and Muthén (2014)</ref> introduced the alignment optimization method, which accommodates a large number of groups but allows only a single categorical covariate.

text.text: Similarly, Bauer (2017) proposed moderated nonlinear factor analysis, which enables the inclusion of both categorical and continuous covariates.
text.formatted: Similarly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bauer (2017)</ref> proposed moderated nonlinear factor analysis, which enables the inclusion of both categorical and continuous covariates.

text.text: In recent years, research on MI has increasingly shifted from CFA-based toward EFAbased approaches, which offer several important advantages.
In CFA models, model misspecification is typically addressed through modification indices, which require iterative respecification and re-estimation.
EFA models, by contrast, allow cross-loadings to be freely estimated and readily incorporated.

Even when configural invariance holds, constraining crossloadings to zero in multifactorial CFA models may be overly restrictive, whereas EFA-based methods can interpret differences in cross-loadings as evidence bearing on metric invariance.
CFA-based approaches also require strong a priori assumptions about the latent structure (Brown, 2015).
text.formatted: CFA-based approaches also require strong a priori assumptions about the latent structure <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Brown, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Although EFA relies on prior knowledge to some degree as well, it is more flexible in capturing the structure underlying the data: rather than restricting items to load only on theoretically expected factors, it permits the examination of alternative loading patterns, thereby providing a more practical framework for evaluating configural and metric invariance.
For further details, see Dolan et al. (2009) and De Roover and Vermunt (2019).
text.formatted: For further details, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Dolan et al. (2009)</ref> and De <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Roover and Vermunt (2019)</ref>.

text.text: In ILSAs, groups are often defined by multiple covariates, both continuous and categorical.
However, EFA-and CFA-based approaches typically test MI for a single covariate at a time, potentially overlooking other relevant covariates and their interactions.

Model-based recursive partitioning (MOB; Zeileis et al., 2008) addresses this limitation by testing whether model parameters remain stable across subgroups defined by covariates, without requiring prior assumptions about group structure.

When parameter instability is detected, the data are recursively partitioned into subgroups, resulting in a tree structure.

text.text: A model is fitted to the full dataset, and its parameters (e.g., factor loadings, inter-factor correlations, and the log-likelihood) are estimated.
Parameter stability is evaluated using structural change tests for each covariate.
If one or more covariates exhibit statistically significant instability (after Bonferroni correction), the covariate with the smallest p-value is selected as the splitting variable.

The procedure is repeated recursively until (a) no further significant splits are detected, (b) a pre-specified maximum tree depth is reached, or (c) the sample size within a node falls below a predefined threshold (Sterner & Goretzko, 2023).

text.text: This algorithm offers several advantages over traditional multigroup approaches such as MGEFA and MGCFA.
First, it accommodates continuous covariates without imposing arbitrary cut-off points.

Second, it can detect interaction effects among covariates: for example, after an initial split by gender, subsequent splits may reveal region-specific differences, thereby identifying non-invariance driven by an interaction (e.g., gender × region).

In recent years, tree-based extensions such as EFA-Tree and CFA-Tree have attracted increasing attention for investigating measurement invariance and identifying sources of heterogeneity (Bulut et al., 2024; Goretzko et al., 2026; Goretzko & Sterner, 2025; Sterner et al., 2024; Sterner & Goretzko, 2023; Straub et al., 2025).

text.text: In these studies, covariates such as age, gender, region, education level, immigration background, and marital status have been used to define subgroups and assess MI, typically under the assumption that invariance violations arise from observed grouping variables.
However, ACQ bias may represent an unobserved source of non-invariance (Sterner et al., 2026).
text.formatted: However, ACQ bias may represent an unobserved source of non-invariance <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Sterner et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: As discussed earlier, ACQ bias can distort the estimation of latent constructs by systematically influencing item responses, inter-item relationships, and item means.
Understanding the sources of ACQ is equally critical.

Although its underlying mechanisms are not fully understood, prior research has linked ACQ to personality traits such as agreeableness (Hibbing et al., 2017) and optimism (Kam & Zhou, 2014), early literacy practices (Bulut, 2021), cultural influences (Bulut et al., 2024; Rammstedt et al., 2013), and subgroup-specific tendencies within the same culture (D' Urso et al., 2023).

text.text: Moreover, certain groups may be particularly prone to ACQ (Van Vaerenbergh & Thomas, 2012), and its magnitude may vary across countries and cultures (Rammstedt et al., 2013).

text.text: Because ACQ bias clearly influences the factor structure, failing to model it makes it impossible to determine whether the results of multigroup comparisons reflect ACQ bias or genuine group differences. Sterner et al. (2026) grouped the potential sources of ACQ into three main domains: (a) respondent characteristics (e.g., agreeableness, age, gender), (b) survey characteristics (e.g., the presence of positively and negatively worded items, survey mode), and (c) cultural characteristics (e.g., social norms).

text.text: Importantly, interactions among these factors may further exacerbate the effects of ACQ.
Taken together, ACQ bias can contaminate the invariance structure of latent constructs across subgroups and act as a hidden source of non-invariance.
Explicitly modeling and controlling for it is therefore essential for determining whether observed group differences reflect substantive variation or methodological artifacts (Sterner et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Explicitly modeling and controlling for it is therefore essential for determining whether observed group differences reflect substantive variation or methodological artifacts <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Sterner et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Existing CFA-and EFAbased approaches typically rely on global model specifications and assume homogeneous parameter structures across individuals or groups.
Tree-based approaches differ fundamentally in that they explicitly model parameter instability across covariates.

Whereas random-intercept (RI) models aim to control method effects through a global correction (e.g., by assuming equal unstandardized factor loadings on a method factor), tree-based methods can identify subgroups with distinct parameter structures.
This makes them particularly well-suited to detecting heterogeneous ACQ patterns and interaction effects that may remain undetected under traditional approaches.

The present study examines whether tree-based factor-analytic approaches, in standard and random-intercept (RI) form, detect group differences in ACQ and, more importantly, whether they attribute measurement heterogeneity to its correct source.

When groups differ in acquiescence, a model without an RI factor can absorb the method variance only into its content parameters, so a difference in response style may be mistaken for metric non-invariance, a concern raised by D' Urso et al. (2023).
text.formatted: When groups differ in acquiescence, a model without an RI factor can absorb the method variance only into its content parameters, so a difference in response style may be mistaken for metric non-invariance, a concern raised by D' <ref type="bibr">Urso et al. (2023)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, when an RI factor is modeled, a genuine difference in the content loadings could be absorbed partly by the RI parameters.
Separating the two sources requires a design in which they are manipulated independently.

We therefore crossed four data-generating conditions (full invariance, non-invariance in ACQ only, non-invariance in the content loadings only, and both) and complemented the tree-based tests with block-wise parameter-instability tests that examine the RI variance and the content loadings separately.
Four methods are compared: EFA-Tree, RI-EFA-Tree, CFA-Tree, and RI-CFA-Tree.

With a single content factor, the exploratory and confirmatory specifications are alternative parameterizations of the same covariance and mean structure, so the comparison of central interest is between each tree and its RI counterpart; the exploratory variants are reported for completeness.

A Monte Carlo simulation crossed the type of heterogeneity with the number of groups, the sample size per group, the number of items, the proportion of reversed items, the proportion of groups in the first cluster, the magnitude of the content-loading difference, and the level of the ACQ loadings.

The methods were evaluated on Type I error, power, the rejection rates of the block-wise tests and the resulting attribution rates, and the recovery of node-specific factor loadings (Tucker's congruence coefficient, bias, and root mean squared error [RMSE]).
text.formatted: The methods were evaluated on Type I error, power, the rejection rates of the block-wise tests and the resulting attribution rates, and the recovery of node-specific factor loadings (Tucker's congruence coefficient, bias, and root mean squared error <ref type="bibr">[RMSE]</ref>).

text.text: The study addresses the following research questions: RQ1: Do tree-based methods, with and without an RI factor, keep the Type I error rate at the nominal level when groups do not differ, although ACQ is present?
RQ2: How well do the standard and RI versions of these methods detect group differences that arise from ACQ only, from the content loadings only, or from both?

RQ3: When heterogeneity is detected, do block-wise parameter-instability tests attribute it to its correct source (RI variance vs. content loadings), and does this depend on how the block test is constructed?

This study aims to compare tree-based factor-analytic methods with and without an RI factor in (a) controlling the Type I error rate when ACQ is present but equal across groups, (b) detecting group differences in ACQ and in the content loadings, and (c) attributing detected heterogeneity to its correct source.
We conducted a Monte Carlo simulation study manipulating the following factors: • Number of groups: GROUPN = {3, 6, 10}.
There is not a common number of groups when we examine cross-cultural research.
However, ILSAs were administered in 81 regions for PISA 2022, and the World Values Survey (Wave 7) was conducted in 66 regions.
Reflecting this diversity also entails significant data collection costs.
For studies without extensive funding, we aimed to mimic smaller numbers of groups to represent small-to medium-scale cross-cultural research.
• Sample size per group: NOBS = {500, 1000}.

We examined the number of items at two levels.

text.text: In this context, we examine the ratio of NW items in the simulated dataset at two levels.

When examining NVAR x BALANCE, for 6-item conditions, there are 2 NW items (6 x0.33 = 1.98) and 3 NW items (6 x0.50 = 3); and for 10-item conditions, 3 items are NW (10 ×0.33 = 3.33) and 5 items are NW (10 ×0.50 = 5).
• Proportion of groups in cluster 1: PROP_GROUP = {0.33, 0.50}.
The first rounded number of groups (GROUPN × PROP_GROUP) formed cluster 1 and the remaining groups formed cluster 2.
For example, with GROUPN = 3, cluster 1 contained one group when PROP_GROUP = 0.33 and two groups when PROP_GROUP = 0.50.
Cluster 1 carried the higher ACQ loadings (themes 2 and 4) and the higher content loadings (themes 3 and 4).
• Type of heterogeneity: TYPE = {invariance, ACQ only, substantive only, both}, referred to as themes 1-4 (Table 1).

text.text: In theme 1, the two clusters had identical population parameters; in theme 2, only the ACQ loadings differed (0.30 in cluster 1 vs.
0.15 in cluster 2); in theme 3, only the content loadings differed; and in theme 4, both differed, in the same cluster.
• ACQ loading level: RILOAD = {0.15, 0.30}.
In themes 1 and 3, the ACQ loadings were equal in both clusters and set to this level; in themes 2 and 4, they were fixed by design at 0.30 (cluster 1) and 0.15 (cluster 2).

• Distractor covariates: three covariates unrelated to the data-generating process were generated for every respondent, following Sterner and Goretzko (2023): cov1, an ordinal variable with ten equiprobable levels (deciles of a standard normal draw); cov2, a binary variable; and cov3, a five-category variable.

text.text: A continuous cov1 was not used because, with up to 10,000 respondents, testing all of its candidate split points was computationally prohibitive.
Factor loadings were not fixed at single values.
In each replication, one uniform offset per item, uj ~ U(-0.05, 0.05), was drawn for the content loadings and another for the ACQ loadings, and added to the level of the item's cluster.

Content loadings therefore followed U(0.65, 0.75), U(0.50, 0.60), or U(0.35, 0.45) for the levels 0.70, 0.55, and 0.40, and ACQ loadings followed U(0.10, 0.20) or U(0.25, 0.35) for the levels 0.15 and 0.30.

Because the offsets were shared by all groups, groups within a cluster had identical population parameters, so that theme 1 was an exact null condition, and the differences between clusters equaled exactly MAGN for the content loadings and 0.15 for the ACQ loadings.
Reversed items had negative content loadings and positive ACQ loadings, and all items were analyzed in their original direction.
Only unidimensional content structures were simulated, and skewness was set to zero.

The data were generated with functions adapted from the latentFactoR package (Christensen et al., 2022), in which the ACQ factor is added as a method factor to the population correlation matrix, so that the item variances are 1 in both clusters.

text.text: A full crossing of all factors would create cells in which a factor has no effect (e.g., MAGN under invariance, or RILOAD in themes 2 and 4, where the ACQ loadings were fixed by design).

These redundant cells were excluded, leaving 24 base cells (GROUPN × NOBS × NVAR × BALANCE) × 18 theme-specific cells = 432 conditions: 96 for theme 1 (RILOAD × PROP_GROUP), 48 for theme 2 (PROP_GROUP), 192 for theme 3 (MAGN × RILOAD × PROP_GROUP), and 96 for theme 4 (MAGN × PROP_GROUP; Table 1).

The minimum node size was ten observations per free parameter (180 to 310 observations, depending on the model and the number of items).
For the EFA-Tree, the unidimensional model was specified as a single-factor EFA block.

In all models, the content factor was identified by fixing its variance to 1, so that all loadings were freely estimated, and item intercepts were included, so that the EFA-and CFAbased trees tested the same parameters.
For the RI-EFA-Tree models, a similar procedure was followed.
In addition to the substantive factor, a method factor representing ACQ bias was incorporated.
The factor loadings of the ACQ factor were fixed across items, and the correlation between the substantive factor and the ACQ factor was constrained to be orthogonal (i.e., fixed at 0.00).
In the RI-EFA-Tree model, the unstandardized factor loadings of the items on the ACQ factor were fixed at 1.00.
The variance of the RI factor was freely estimated.
CFA-Tree models were specified as a unidimensional CFA with the same estimator, identification, mean structure, and tree settings as the EFA-Tree.
With one content factor and no cross-loadings, the EFA and CFA specifications are equivalent, so the two trees can differ only through numerical aspects of estimation.
For the RI-CFA-Tree models, a similar procedure was followed.
In addition to the substantive factor, a method factor representing ACQ was modeled.
The factor loadings of the ACQ factor were fixed across items, and the correlation between the substantive factor and the ACQ factor was constrained to be orthogonal (i.e., fixed at 0.00).
In the RI-CFA-Tree model, the unstandardized factor loadings of the items on the ACQ factor were fixed at 1.00.
The fixed loading specification for the ACQ factor followed the conventional RI formulation.

Variability in ACQ effects was introduced at the data-generating stage rather than at the model-estimation stage, allowing evaluation of how well RI-based approaches recovered heterogeneous method effects.
As in the RI-EFA-Tree, the RI variance was freely estimated.
A split shows that some parameters differ between subgroups, but not which ones.

To examine the source of heterogeneity, we tested the stability of two parameter blocks of the full-sample model across GROUP and across each distractor covariate: the RI variance (RI models only) and the content loadings.
These tests apply the score-based tests of measurement invariance (Merkle & Zeileis, 2013; Wang et al., 2014) to a subset of the parameters and were computed alongside the trees, not as part of them.

text.text: Because each decorrelated column is a linear combination of the scores of all parameters, a difference in one block can propagate into the test of another.
The efficient block test instead removes from the scores of B their projection on the scores of A, using the expected information matrix Î:
To first order, instability in A then leaves the test of B unaffected.

Attribution was scored for the RI models in each replication: it was correct when the RI-variance test rejected if and only if the groups differed in ACQ (themes 2 and 4) and the content-loading test rejected if and only if they differed in the content loadings (themes 3 and 4).
A rejection for a block whose parameters did not differ between groups was counted as misattribution.
Because such a block rejects at the nominal rate, the attainable maximum of correct attribution is about .95 in themes 2 and 3, .952 ≈ .90 in theme 1, and close to 1 in theme 4.
The projected score is Neyman's (1959) efficient score for the tested block, that is, the part of its score that is orthogonal to the scores of the remaining parameters.

text.text: With normal-theory ML, the expected Hessian depends on the data only through their first two moments, so the expected information used in the projection is appropriate for five-point items as long as the mean and covariance structure is correctly specified; departures from normality affect the variance of the projected scores, which the robust estimate takes into account.
Two limits of this first-order argument should be noted.
If the model is misspecified, the observed information is a natural alternative for the projection.

If groups differ in their item means, the expected covariance scores differ between the groups even when the covariance parameters are equal, so tests of covariance-structure blocks should then be computed after centering the items within the levels of the covariate.
Neither situation arises in the simulation, in which the item means did not differ between groups; both are examined in the empirical example.
In a toy example, we illustrate what the trees and the block-wise tests report when groups differ only in acquiescence.

The data were generated with the simulation code for one theme-2 condition: a unidimensional construct measured by six five-point items and three groups of 500 respondents each (N = 1,500), with Groups A and B showing low and Group C high ACQ.

Two data sets were generated with the same random seed and differed only in keying: in the first, two of the six items were reversed (unbalanced keying, BALANCE = 0.33); in the second, three items were reversed (balanced keying, BALANCE = 0.50).
The standardized population factor loadings are presented in Table 2.

text.text: Groups A and B therefore had identical population parameters, and Group C differed from them only in its ACQ loadings, by 0.15 for every item, so that metric invariance held for the content factor but not for the ACQ factor.
Reversed items had negative content loadings and positive ACQ loadings, and all items were analyzed in their original direction.

The grouping variable was included as a partitioning covariate together with the three distractor covariates of the simulation: an ordinal variable with ten equiprobable levels (e.g., a socio-economic status decile), a binary variable (e.g., gender), and a five-category variable (e.g., educational status).
Each data set is a single replication: it shows what the methods report, whereas the simulation shows how often they are right, and the corresponding simulation rates are reported below.

text.text: The methods were evaluated on three groups of measures.

Detection: in theme 1, the proportions of trees that split on any variable, on GROUP, and on a distractor covariate (Type I error); in themes 2-4, the proportion of trees that split on GROUP (power) and the adjusted Rand index (ARI) between the terminal nodes and the true clusters.
Splits on a distractor covariate were counted as Type I errors in all themes; in themes 2-4 these are per-tree rates that include the tests in the child nodes.
Attribution: the rejection rates of the two block-wise tests on GROUP and the rate of correct attribution defined above.
Recovery: Tucker's congruence coefficient, bias, and RMSE of the node-specific content loadings.

text.text: Three covariates served as partitioning variables: gender (male, female), age, grouped into 18-30, 31-45, and 46-65 years and treated as an ordered factor, and country.
Respondents younger than 18 or older than 65, with another gender category, or from countries with fewer than 500 respondents were excluded.

The final sample comprised N = 26,236 respondents from Australia (1,676), Canada (2,145), Germany (555), Great Britain (4,913), India (1,107), the Philippines (700), and the United States (15,140); 16,351 were aged 18-30, 5,991 were aged 31-45, and 3,894 were aged 46-65, and 61.6% (16,164) were female.

The items were analyzed in their original direction with the models, estimator, identification, and tree settings of the simulation (ML, factor variance fixed to 1, freely estimated RI variance, Bonferroni-corrected α = .05, and a minimum node size of ten observations per free parameter, i.e., 300 for EFAtree and CFAtree and 310 for riEFAtree and riCFAtree).

Because the earlier EFA-based trees did not include a mean structure, we grew all four trees once with the item intercepts, as in the simulation, and once without them (covariance structure only; minimum node sizes 200 and 210), that is, eight trees in total.
Block-wise tests were computed at the root and at every inner node for the RI variance, the content loadings, the intercepts, and the residual variances.

Because the factor mean and variance are fixed in every node, a difference in the factor variance between subgroups appears as a proportional change of all loadings, a difference in the factor mean as a shift of the intercepts proportional to the loadings, and a difference in mean acquiescence as a uniform shift of all intercepts.

We therefore reparametrized the two blocks so that these directions became separate coordinates and tested each part with the efficient test: the factor-variance direction and the remaining, non-proportional loading differences (metric noninvariance; 9 parameters), and the factor-mean direction, the uniform intercept shift, and the remaining intercept differences (scalar non-invariance; 8 parameters).

In a check with 500 replications of continuous data per condition (three groups of 1,000 respondents, ten balanced items), the two remaining parts held the nominal level when the groups differed only in the factor mean, the factor variance, or mean acquiescence (rejection rates .028-.056) and rejected in all replications for their own source; without any group difference, all parts rejected in .024-.076 of the replications.
The RI-variance test rejected in at most 5.2% of the replications under the other sources but in 63.6% when mean acquiescence differed.

In another 500 replications per condition, centering the items within groups reduced this rate from .596 to .048 (no group difference: .044), whereas a difference in the RI variance was still detected in all replications; the covariance-block tests were therefore also computed after centering the items within the levels of each covariate.

The directional parts, in contrast, also absorbed non-uniform differences: the uniform shift was rejected in 97.4% of the replications when two items had higher intercepts, so it is not specific to mean acquiescence.

With N = 26,236, nearly every test is significant; we therefore compared the parts by their χ 2 value per degree of freedom, which indicates the strength of the evidence rather than the size of a difference, and report country-specific riCFA estimates as descriptive magnitudes.
Because the empirical model is likely to be somewhat misspecified, all tests were repeated with the observed instead of the expected information.
We first report convergence and admissibility, then Type I error (theme 1), the detection of heterogeneity (themes 2-4), its attribution, and the recovery of the factor loadings.

All trees and all full-sample models converged in every replication.

With the efficient test, riCFAtree attributed heterogeneity to its correct source.

When only ACQ differed, the RI block was rejected in all replications and the content-loading block in 5.1%; when only the content loadings differed, the content-loading block was rejected in 99.9% and the RI block in 5.7% of the replications; and when both differed, both blocks were rejected in 99.8% of the replications.

The standard block test, in contrast, attributed a large part of purely substantive non-invariance to acquiescence: in theme 3, it rejected the RI block in 78.5% of the replications, so that only 12.8% were correctly attributed, and in theme 4 it missed one of the two differences in 41% of the replications.

This misattribution grew with the size of the loading difference and with the amount of information in the data, from .58 (three groups of 500) to .94 (ten groups of 1,000), and reached .99 for a .30 loading shift with ACQ loadings of .15 (Figure 4).

India and the Philippines differed from the Western countries in the variance of the RI, as expected from cross-cultural research on acquiescence, but also in the level of self-esteem, in the factor variance, and in intercept differences beyond a uniform shift; the uniform shift itself may reflect mean acquiescence or scalar non-invariance common to all items.

That the trees without an RI factor and without intercepts also separated India and the Philippines first agrees with these additional differences in the covariance structure, and not with a pure acquiescence difference, which the simulation showed to be nearly invisible to such trees under balanced keying.
The first split on age in the trees that tested the intercepts was dominated by the loading-proportional intercept direction.

This is consistent with impact, that is, a difference in the latent mean, but without anchor items it cannot be distinguished from intercept bias proportional to the loadings, just as a uniform shift cannot be attributed to mean acquiescence rather than to scalar non-invariance common to all items.

text.text: This study examined whether model-based trees with and without a random intercept detect group differences in acquiescence and attribute measurement heterogeneity to its correct source.
Three findings stand out.
First, when groups differed only in acquiescence, trees without an RI factor either mistook this difference for metric non-invariance or missed it.

With unbalanced keying, CFAtree split on GROUP in about two thirds of the replications and its content-loading block was rejected in more than three quarters, so that a pure response-style difference appeared as a difference in the content structure; with balanced keying, the same difference was practically invisible to the tree (power .02).
Second, riCFAtree detected acquiescence differences with high power regardless of keying and kept the Type I error rate at the nominal level when ACQ was present but equal across groups.

Third, attributing a detected difference to its source required an appropriate block-wise test: the efficient test attributed heterogeneity correctly at its attainable maximum, whereas the standard approach of selecting a block from the fully decorrelated scores attributed up to 99% of purely substantive non-invariance to acquiescence, and did so more often as the sample size and the number of groups increased.
The dependence on keying follows from how ACQ enters the data.
In the data-generating model, a larger ACQ loading adds roughly the same positive amount to the covariances of all item pairs, regardless of keying, while the item variances remain unchanged.

With unbalanced keying, a one-factor model absorbs part of this shift into its loadings, inflating positively keyed and attenuating reversed loadings, so that the ACQ difference appears as metric non-invariance.

With balanced keying, the shift is not captured by the content parameters: the content-loading block of CFAtree was rejected at close to the nominal rate (.068), so the pseudo-true loadings hardly differed between the clusters and the tree had nothing to detect.
Both patterns are consistent with the observation that acquiescence distorts factor solutions in a keying-dependent way (D' Urso et al., 2023; Ferrando & Lorenzo-Seva, 2010; Savalei & Falk, 2014).
text.formatted: Both patterns are consistent with the observation that acquiescence distorts factor solutions in a keying-dependent way (D' <ref type="bibr">Urso et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Ferrando & Lorenzo-Seva, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Savalei & Falk, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The RI factor captures the shift directly through its variance, which explains why the power and the estimates of riCFAtree did not depend on keying balance.
The failure of the standard block test has a related cause.
In the RI model, the scores of the RI variance and of the content loadings are correlated, because a uniform change in the loadings also changes the average covariance among the items.
Decorrelating all scores and then selecting a block mixes the blocks, so that a difference in the loadings leaks into the test of the RI variance, the more so the more information the data contain.

Projecting out the remaining parameters before testing removed this leakage without a loss of power: the efficient test rejected the loading block more often than the standard test when the loadings did differ (.999 vs. .805 in theme 3).
The empirical example, based on a scale with balanced keying, shows how the block-wise tests change the interpretation of a tree.

All trees detected heterogeneity, and the RI loadings were considerably higher in the nodes comprising Indian and Filipino respondents (.26-.34) than in the Western nodes (.17-.22), a pattern consistent with cross-cultural research showing that acquiescence is weaker in more individualistic and more economically developed countries (Johnson et al., 2005; Rammstedt et al., 2017; Smith, 2004).

text.text: The block-wise tests, however, located acquiescence differences only between countries: the RI variance did not differ between age groups or genders, and the first split on age in the trees that tested the intercepts was dominated by the direction of a latent mean difference.
The country difference in the RI variance survived centering the items within countries and the use of the observed information.
Even between countries, acquiescence was one of several sources, together with differences in the factor mean and variance and in the intercepts.

This agrees with the simulation, in which a pure acquiescence difference under balanced keying was nearly invisible to trees without an RI factor; that such trees nevertheless split by country first points to the additional differences that the block tests identified.
In empirical data, a split should therefore not be read as evidence of measurement non-invariance, let alone of acquiescence, before its source has been examined.
Several practical implications follow.

First, when a scale contains both positively and negatively worded items, analyzing the items in their original direction with an RI factor is necessary for interpreting tree-based invariance results: without it, a group difference in acquiescence can appear as metric non-invariance (unbalanced keying) or remain undetected (balanced keying).
Second, neither a split nor a rejection of the loading block in a model without an RI factor should be taken as evidence of substantive non-invariance when the groups may differ in acquiescence.

Third, the source of a detected difference should be examined with block-wise tests that project out the remaining parameters, as the efficient test does; testing a subset of the fully decorrelated scores (e.g., the parm argument of strucchange::sctest) can attribute substantive differences to acquiescence, and larger samples make this error more likely, not less.

Because the trees fix the factor mean and variance in every node, group differences in these latent parameters (impact) also produce splits; separating their directions from the loading and intercept blocks, as in the empirical example, prevents impact from being read as non-invariance.

Fourth, researchers should report node-specific estimates, including the RI loadings, alongside the tree; report the bias of loadings by keying direction, because errors of opposite sign cancel in the average; and decide a priori whether item intercepts are to be tested, because including them changes the splitting variables, as the empirical example illustrates.

Finally, in large samples score-based tests detect trivial differences, so interpreting primarily the upper-level splits and using stricter stopping rules, such as a larger minimum node size or a lower significance level, remains advisable.
Several limitations should be noted.

First, ACQ heterogeneity was operationalized as a difference in the ACQ loadings, that is, in the variance of the RI, with item variances held constant and without group differences in mean acquiescence.

Real differences in acquiescence may also raise item variances and means, which trees without an RI factor could detect through the residual variances and intercepts; the finding that balanced keying hides acquiescence differences from such trees is therefore specific to this covariance-only form.

Second, only one content-loading level in the reference cluster (.70) and two keying ratios (one third and one half reversed items) were studied; misattribution may be larger with weaker loadings were not examined.

Third, substantive non-invariance shifted all loadings by the same amount, which is close to a difference in factor variance; partial non-invariance affecting only some items may be harder to separate from acquiescence.
Fourth, with a single content factor the exploratory and confirmatory trees coincide, so the study cannot speak to the advantages of EFA-based trees in multidimensional structures.
Fifth, five-point items were analyzed as continuous by ML, which produced a constant attenuation of the loadings of about .03.

Sixth, in theme 4 both differences affected the same cluster, so attribution could be assessed only with the block-wise tests, not with the tree structure; moreover, the efficient block test, although it held its nominal level throughout, has not been examined beyond the present design.

Finally, in the empirical example the four-point items were treated as continuous, the results are based on a single dataset with a highly unequal distribution of respondents across countries, and the decomposition of the loading and intercept blocks was checked only in a small simulation with continuous items; its directional parts are not specific (e.g., a uniform intercept shift cannot be distinguished from scalar non-invariance that affects all items alike).
